The image shows split soybean stems with:
- **White/light pith** inside when cut lengthwise
- **Small black specks** scattered on the external stem surface
- Dry, dead stem tissue

Key differential: White pith = SDS (not Brown Stem Rot which has brown pith). The black specks on exterior could also suggest Diaporthe or Charcoal Rot. Let me check references.

Key observations so far:
- Split soybean stems showing **white pith** inside - key SDS diagnostic feature
- Black specks on exterior of stems
- Charcoal Rot reference (top-left) looked similar but its pith should be reddish-brown per description

The white pith strongly points to **Sudden_death_syndrome**. Let me now read the Attractor Guide.

SDS is flagged as over-predicted (16x). Main alternatives: Brown_Stem_Rot (4x), Diaporthe (2x). I need to verify more carefully. Key: the white pith in the test image is the strongest diagnostic sign.

Fusarium reference shows brown vascular tissue internally - doesn't match the white pith in the test image.

**Final analysis:**

| Disease | Pith color | External specks | Match? |
|---|---|---|---|
| SDS | **White** | Blue-green spores on roots | Strong match |
| Brown Stem Rot | Brown | None noted | No - pith wrong |
| Charcoal Rot | Reddish-brown | Black microsclerotia (charcoal) | No - pith wrong |
| Diaporthe | Normal/brown | Black pycnidia in linear rows | No |
| Fusarium | Brown vascular | None noted | No |

The test image shows **split soybean stems with distinctly white pith** - this is the textbook diagnostic feature of SDS: "SDS-infected plants have white pith when stems are cut, distinguishing it from brown stem rot which causes brown pith discoloration." The black specks externally don't negate this - they may be secondary organisms on a dead SDS-infected plant.

Despite the attractor warning, no other class in the list produces white pith when stems are split. BSR (4x alternative) would have brown pith.
